unsupported_claims: The AI frames the trade-off as expressiveness/representational power versus tractability, rather than the paper's computational efficiency versus predictive accuracy.

The AI claims a supervised procedure needs no separate pretraining stage and has lower training-time complexity per task, whereas the paper says supervised learning has high training time complexity due to a blowup in parameters.

The AI describes unsupervised procedures as generally requiring more training time with layer-wise or two-stage pipelines, contradicting the paper's statement that unsupervised optimization is computationally efficient.
The AI claims unsupervised features have lower predictive accuracy, whereas the paper says carefully designed unsupervised objectives closely match task-specific approaches in accuracy.
The AI attributes examples such as autoencoders, RBMs, and reconstruction/generative objectives to the papers, which the evidence does not mention.
rationale: The AI answer inverts the paper's central comparison: the paper says supervised methods have high training-time cost but good accuracy, while unsupervised methods are computationally efficient and can closely match task-specific accuracy. The AI instead claims supervised training is cheaper and unsupervised features are less accurate, which the evidence contradicts.
